utterances.text: Yes, that is 6. That is in. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): Dr. Greve, if you had received this document as a member of the Commission of Experts, would there be some additional information you would want to know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first question would be when is it dated, when was it compiled, by whom would it have been compiled? Is it one document or is this a set of different documents put together? Have they been put together at different times? Have there been added information on them after the originals were produced? I do know, and I should perhaps take this opportunity to mention it if I have not been exact on this before, that the prisoners or the detainees in Omarska and Keraterm, some of them had been taken to the police station in Prijedor or to the military barracks close to Urije or an area an extension of Prijedor town prior to coming to Omarska. In all these four locations, the two camps, Omarska, Keraterm, the police station in Prijedor and the military barracks in Prijedor, so-called "informative talks" were taking place. I do know that a number of people were asked to sign lists of paper and it is my understanding from reading the reports, many of which are newspaper articles from the Serb authorities, that they learned about weaponry through informative talks. So I also wonder, which are the conditions under which someone has signed these lists?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Simo Drljaca one of the officials in 1992 who was in charge of the overall operation of the camp and the informative talks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that Simo Drljaca is now the head of the Prijedor police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that one of the informations to sustain that claim would be that Simo Drljaca is actually the one who signed what is called Exhibit D7. So he was then Chief of Police. This entrance permit to the camp is signed by him and that is the investigation centre. There is every information he was head of police. He was a member of the Krizni Stab. He was a key person then. He was then promoted as of April 1993 to move on to Bijeljina where the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska was located, but he has later moved back into Prijedor and it is my understanding that he is still with the Ministry of Interior but now with another branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the documents that are contained in exhibit D6 were in the possession of Simo Drljaca before they were turned over to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that has been the case, but it could, of course, have been in the hand of an assistant or been on a shelf, but he was the man in charge then and now. So, obviously, he could have had a close look at this before they were handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to the information you indicated you would want to know before making an assessment of what D6 represented, would you also want to know some information about any of the weapons allegedly listed on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I would want a proper translation of all the information which I cannot read myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would it be helpful to know the age of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would indeed be very important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The condition of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and also the question of ammunition if that was available together with these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, I appreciate you are not here as an expert on weaponry in former Yugoslavia, but is it your understanding that the JNA was a well equipped army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Particularly when it came to heavy weaponry such as artillery, yes, but the JNA at this time, meaning the Serbian controlled entity, had almost all the good quality weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that conscripts in the JNA could generally expect to get a weapon, to be issued a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn, if you would, to A/1/88; does that indicate the village of Arifagici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As you turn the page are there approximately 95 names listed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Out of those 95 names, how many have a weapon, whatever that weapon is or whatever its condition may be or however much ammunition may have been provided for it, listed against their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I read everything that is listed next to a name as meaning a weapon, and I will do as a matter of convenience as I am not able to say that some may not be a weapon, I see 10 added information, pieces of information, that could be weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Out of the 95 names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That it is not your understanding, is it, of the way the JNA was equipped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my understanding, everyone in the JNA had at least one normally more weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you see any references here to issuing of canon or heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen none, but again I must apologise that there could be a name I am unable to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, you may be excused -- excuse me, I forgot about you. Go ahead, Dr. Greve. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I had four questions I wanted to ask you, doctor. The first one is, do you know anything about the signs that we saw in the portion of the video that was shown of Kozarac which consisted of on the houses a circle with a cross inside? Very many of the destroyed houses seemed to have them. Do you know anything of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and I included with it actually in my report on Prijedor. It is a circle with an X inside it and it is frequently in blue, and it is understood that this was a marking placed on every house that after the initial attack and the initial destruction was to be further destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then in part of your evidence talking of the various political parties, you said "... and there were some leftist parties, the Reformists, the Liberals". I did not know whether those two were within the group of leftist parties because the names sound unlikely or whether they were additional to the "some leftist parties"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My intention was to present it clearly as being within the leftist group. "Reformed" in this context means reformed communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And "Liberals"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And "Liberals" was also a word used for a leftist party, your Honour. That is my understanding, but I have not gone deep into the background to these parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then in describing Mihajlovic and his Chetniks, would you agree that he is a very controversial figures and that amongst reputable western historians he is very variously regarded as a hero or a villain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fully agree that that is the position among western historical experts. My basic reference is to his position vis-a-vis the partisans. They saw it needed to break with him. It was one of their most important declarations at Jajce in 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Lastly, and this is something you may not be able to help me on at all, we hear so much about ethnic cleansing -- that means in this context moving the Muslims out of a particular area -- and yet you also talk of the refusal to allow Muslims to leave. How are the two reconciled? Why was there not an eagerness that they should leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am guessing, your Honour, I do not know, but to me it comes across as if they were afraid that if people were let out of the area they would eventually want to come back home. This is my understanding. I may in this context add that in 1942, that is, during World War II, in Banja Luka there was a lawyer -- his name has slipped my mind just at the moment -- he was associated with Drazan Mihajlovic, and he is making some references to cleansing and ethnic cleansing, and at that time he is proposing that cleansing would mean to remove, ask people to leave the area, send Croats to Croatia, he is saying Muslims to Turkey, etc. but at this modern -- well, it is not modern -- in the present situation of ethnic cleansing in opstina Prijedor, people were literally prevented from getting out for one reason or another; it could have been that they do not want them back, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, may I know how long you served as an expert on the Commission of Experts and who was the Chairperson when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the Commission of Experts being appointed at 19th October 1993. I started working on 21st October 1993. I came in as the previous Chairman had died, Torkel Ophsahl also a Norwegian, and in the first session after I was appointed it was also confirmed that the Secretary General appointed Cherif Bassiouni as the new Chairman of the Commission of Experts. Officially, the Commission of Experts ended its work by end of April 1993. That is to say, we were in this work for about six months. However, we had to submit the brief report by then. I made the analysis of Prijedor and submitted it on 6th -- excuse me, on 16th June 1993 and the final annex 5, which the report on Prijedor is, was finished in terms of having taken out names and allegations, particularly names of victims, was finished at the Easter time, 1995. But I have remained interested in the issue and I have on many occasions been approached by people whom I am asked or they have asked me to submit material to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have additional questions in the light of these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, once again thank you for coming. You are permanently excused unless I hear an objection -- no. Then you are permanently excused. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, or who will call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be calling the next witness. Before we proceed, we have a housekeeping matter which I think will actually be of some interest to the court. The Prosecution wishes to produce and admit into evidence a model of Omarska which the Defence has had an opportunity to view, which we both think will be of considerable assistance to the court and will expedite matters considerably. So if it would be an appropriate time, I would like to bring it in. One reason I wanted to mention it at the outset is that, under some circumstances, I believe it is going to be helpful to use overhead cameras to view inside the model, at least for the court's benefit. I believe for the next witness, whether or not the cameras are set up, that will not substantially impair the value of his testimony vis-a-vis the model, but for later witnesses where we are focusing more on particular parts of the camp, I think we will want to do that, so the sooner we get to it, the better.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is no objection to the model coming in and that will be an exhibit and it will receive a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to bring it in before the witness come.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In terms of the overhead, are you saying that the cameras have to be adjusted at some point and the question is whether they should be adjusted now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have worked already with the video technicians. To some extent, the current cameras are helpful, but it appears that there will be a need for one or tw additional cameras probably placed in about this point, and I gather they have the equipment to do so. But I think it would be helpful for them to know that the court wishes them to do so in order to aid viewing of the model.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You think we have a lot of pull, do you not!

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I still do not understand; we can go ahead with the next witness. You can bring in the model if there is no objection. It will come in as an exhibit. We will go ahead with the next witness. I do not think how long that witness will need. You may have an objection and I will get to that. Will the cameras have to be moved and reinstalled for the witness after this next one? Is that what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. If I recall the witness order correctly, I think we will have at least a week or two weeks to have the cameras set up in order to use the model properly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see. Then in a week's time even we can encourage that the cameras be installed. Very good. Now about the model, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has no objection against using the model, but we identified at least on one point that it is not correct. It might be totally irrelevant so we reserve our right that if it comes any specific part of that model to object against the correctness of the model. We expressed this already on one single point to the Prosecutor, and we do not think at this moment that it might be relevant, but it may become relevant and then we will point at the incorrectness of the model.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have anything to say? The model then can come in except, as I understand, you will have an objection to some portions of it, perhaps, at a later time. So again, since this is a trial at least to the court, I presume that even though we may have seen some section that later on there is an objection to, we would disregard that; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we might object if it comes to a certain point and we will say, "The model is not correct in this aspect" and, therefore, we object then against using it for that particular reason at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that is well taken. We are not offering the model as the exact representation of Omarska in each and every detail and individual respect. It is clearly accurate enough to be of considerable assistance in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then what number will that be?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What number will that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 130, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you want to bring the model in now before the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. 130 then will be admitted. Mr. Niemann, Judge Stephen has just raised a question about the exhibits that were offered today. On the index to the documents that were to be tendered by the Prosecution on page 3, there was a change in the numbering of the exhibits beginning with, I think, 123. 123 became 126 and there were some other numbers. I think all of this was occasioned because of a question perhaps by me. In any case, would you please submit a new list for the Trial Chamber with the correct listing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think the Chamber will take its recess now and then you can finish putting the model together and Defence will be able to look at it to make sure it is at least put together properly. I understand there are objections. So we will return 20 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Before we begin, it is not necessary but you may wish me to explain quickly the logistics of using this in case the court has any questions about it. As you might have been able to see earlier, the model can be taken apart for various purposes but primarily to show the inside of the structures. So, you can take off the roof and show the upper storey of each building, and then the upper storey can be removed in addition to show the entire ground floor. So that whatever portion of the camp may be relevant to any particular witness's testimony, it can be displayed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution's next witness is (redacted) (redacted) called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take the oath there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath? Would you read the oath and take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you tell the court your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that where you lived your entire life until the conflict in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell the court during what periods of time you were defined in those particular ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until 1974 when a new constitution was adopted, to us, Muslims, we were not allowed to declare ourselves as Muslims, but we were forced by political measures to be either Serbs, Croats, Montenegrins, Slovenes or, if we did not want any of those, we had the possibility to be unspecified. After 1974 it was possible to be a Muslim, not as religious belonging, but as a National belonging. The only difference was that the religion was with a small letter; whereas the National belonging was with a capital "N". Neither theoretically nor practically did I agree with the use of a name of a religion for a national group, so I decided to be a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the period of time you were growing up in opstina Prijedor, up to about the time of the elections, what were relations like between the ethnic groups in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would simply say that they were excellent, and that at no time we could see differences between nationalities. Never has anyone asked anybody else, "To which nationality do you belong?" -- at least where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did people associate only with members of the same national group or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, never -- no, I cannot really say "never", there would be people who would choose a friend and it would be somebody who was from the same nationality, but that was neither the rule or the principle that people would be friends according to and socialise according to their nationality. The only way one would choose a friend was according to the personal characteristics and values and not according to somebody's nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did people from the different ethnic groups attend each other's religious or cultural festivals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Personally, as many of my friends, I used to go to almost all the Serbian festivals and then they would come to -- the Serbs would come to the religious festivals of Muslims and I used to go to the midnight mass organised by Catholics at Christmas. I had a friend who is now a priest and I used to go to the orthodox church to ring the bells there, so we respected one another. We respected all religions that existed in the area where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did people associate together on those formal occasions, like parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe in that region we liked socialising, associating, friendships. Reasons were found just to be together, be it sport events or cultural events or politics, less in political events, but the mentality was such, it was depending on what people liked really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you bring a tape with you that contains footage, home video footage, of a party at which Serbs, Muslims and Croats are associating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to show that tape now, your Honour, as Exhibit 131 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has the Defence seen the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 131?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 131 will be admitted. MR. TIEGER (To the witness): (redacted), as the tape is being shown perhaps you can help us out by pointing out who belongs to which ethnic group as they appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I cannot see. I do not know where to turn in order to be able to see. I cannot see anything. Could you tell me what button I should press, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Silvije Saric have a political position in -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Saric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he involved in any political party in and, if so, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the President or the Chairman of the HDZ at Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Slobodan Kurozovic, was he involved with any political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the SDS party in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions about the nature of the ethnic communities in Prijedor. Was the Muslim community of Prijedor a fundamentalist community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. Never. I never noticed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For example, how many people would you submit would go regularly to religious services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five to eight per cent, and the oldest people, the elderly, would usually go to the mosques on Fridays at noon. I could see a small group wearing French type of berets that would pray and then go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about the Serbian community, was that a strongly observant religious community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not notice that. They did not observe it too much, the Serbs. There was a church in the centre of the town, and I would see rarely a younger person. They are usually elderly people and those who really did want to go there and abide by their religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the time you were growing up was religion any sort of barrier between the individual citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could notice, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We noted that you were able to point out on the tape who was Serb, who was Muslim, who was Croat; were you able to do that because you knew those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only because I knew them, only because I knew them personally, and I know that they belong to a particular nationality, that is, and a particular religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there some ways of recognising who was a member of a particular ethnic group if you did not know them? Did first or last names, for example, indicate whether or not someone was a member of a particular group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one could know that according to their names and first names, much less according to the last names. The Muslims names were very characteristic and different than the first names of Serbs and Croats. But when one came to last names, there were many cases that the same last name was to be found among the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there also some last names which were distinctively Serb, Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Muslim that could be a bit more true; for example, Beglerbegovic, Hadzimustavic, Hadziahmetovic, Ahmetovic or Nezirovic. Some last names were really characteristic only for that nationality; whereas for the Serb and Croatian nationality it was very difficult to say. There was a case when I was with a friend and his name is Blazo and I was constantly telling him "Blaz". Then at some stage he said: "Why do you call me Blaz? My name is not Blaz". I said: "How?" "My name is Blazo". I said: "What is the difference?" And he said: "'Blaz' is a Croat whereas 'Blazo' is a Serb". There were so many very small differences. I also know of another case when we were discussing names, we would be discussing very often things. The Croatian names, for example, they are all the same in Croatian and Serbian names except for "Ivan" and "Jovan". "Jovan" is a name you cannot find among Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that true for the younger generation than for the older generations in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A great difference. Young people were more progressive. They wanted to go to the west. Modernisation came and greater economic emancipation, progress, disco clubs, videos, new technical equipment, contemporary films and they started to give names according to TV series, films, some sports personality or cultural personalities. I know at Kozarac, for example, there was somebody called "Dejvi" or "Glen" Ahil. There was even a name "Genije". "Dejvi" was with me at Manjaca; "Glen" was with me at Omarska. Then you could find "Irena", "Sanja" or "Dijana". These were the names in our regions, some new more modern names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we show the party in 1990? Perhaps we could run the next tape and see the,...how people were associating in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again can you point out who is Serbo-Croat and Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb, a Muslim, and this is a Muslim woman married to a Serb, then a Muslim. A Muslim, this is a Croat and a Serb. This is a Serb, a Croat, a Muslim. A Serb woman. His name is Djuro, then Josip. He is a Serb married to a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we stop the tape, please? (redacted) in the interests of time, that party from 1990 continues; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to clarify that. (To the witness): The tape indicator showed 1990, is that the correct date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is 1991 in February. There is such video tape here from February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The party from 1990 that we saw, does it continue and show dancing and drinking and general party festivities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you could see that was in February '91. We met once again and we were more numerous then. I think there were more than 200 or 300 people there. What is important here, these are real representatives from Prijedor, and we all loved nature. There was at the Mountain Kozara, there was a mountain refuge there. We would not look at who belonged to what kind of a profession or what nationality; people who loved to associate and who loved nature would go to that refuge and that was chosen so that people from all walks of life would meet, engineers, teachers, hairdressers. So the love for the nature was not determined by any kind of national or religious structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I bring your attention now to 1990 when the elections were held. Before that time what kind of system was there in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that time there was the socialist communist system. I could not determine that precisely because I am not an expert for that matter, but the communists were in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the system of communism began to break down eventually in 1990 democratic elections were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the time of that election, did you become aware at the beginning of any nationalist movement within former Yugoslavia as the communist system began to break down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With which ethnic groups or what ethnic group was that movement associated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I saw that such movements appeared in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the media, television, newspapers, radio and other, but mostly through newspapers and television.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were some of the leaders or promoters of that movement as you came to learn of it through the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand that question. Do you mean politicians or who were people who did that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, who were politicians associated with that nationalist movement before the time of the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the elections a man No. 1 was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there others associated with that nationalist movement as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were others too. If I may, I should like to go back even before Milosevic emerged: there were various things, publication of books with nationalistic content such as, for instance, "The Knife" by Vuk Draskovic -- I read that book -- then "Golubnjaca"; then poet, Rajka Petrov Nogo; Lubarda, painter, who ended up in Belgrade, and who were saying that Bosnia was a dark land for them, dark (indecipherable); then the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts appeared and said about the peril threatening the Serb people, and then Milosevic entered the scene and after he visit to Kosovo and his famous centres, and "Nobody may beat you", he became the most popular person among the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Draskovic, did he advocate an expanded or greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did greater Serbia mean? Did it indicate the borders of that entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read books on history. The Serbs always indicated that Czar Dusan, their great Czar, in the remote history who at the time created the largest estate in the Balkans. Then for two years, or perhaps for a year, a year and a half or two years, I happened to come across a Belgrade magazine called "Praticna Jurna" and I saw the map of greater Serbia. That map covered Serbia, then the corridors, Slavonia, and then Krajina towards Croatia, then out to, access to Karlovac and then to the coast, into the Adriatic. In the beginning such phenomena in Yugoslavia such as, for instance, that all Serbs had to live in one state, it sounded rather incredible. People did not take it seriously but it began to gain momentum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the media show events or rallies at which Serbian nationalism or a greater Serbia was promoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were those rallies held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More often than not such rallies took place in Serbia. There was a huge rally at Gazimestan in Kosovo, then another one in Belgrade at the mouth of the Sava into the Danube. It was announced very pompously as the rally of 1 million people. In Prijedor, I met (redacted) (redacted) who told me, more or less confidentially, in confidence, or I could not quite understand what he was saying, he said: "Tomorrow morning we shall be leaving with two or three buses to bring down the unprincipled coalition". Then a Serb rally was to be held in Ljubljana in Slovenia and that was also announced in the press: "We shall go; we shall hold it; we are off". I must say, I said some misgivings, I feared incidents or something, but then it was cancelled. I do not know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did some of the Serbs from Prijedor manifest an interest in these rallies or attend these rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the exception of what this (redacted) told me, that they were going to overthrow the unprincipled coalition, in practice, in life itself, I did not feel anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were symbols displayed at these rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and what came as a surprise to me because we, the former Yugoslavia, were a country of partisans, a country which liberated itself, which fought against fascism and after the war as a child I was, after World War II I mean, I was brought up and educated in the spirit of communism, partisan victories. At that time at school and always I said that apart from fascists our enemies were domestic traitors, Ustase and Chetniks. When I saw Chetnik symbols which was publicly brandished at the rallies or being sold around, a group I should say of professional rally-goers headed by a gentleman called Solevic, that was his family name, simply it was beyond me. How could it be that those Chetniks, those domestic traitors whose leader was Draza Mihajlvic, a pronounced traitor and a criminal, could be rehabilitated in such a manner all of a sudden, and how could his symbols be embraced by Serbs who bore the brunt of the fight of the struggling in World War II. It came as a surprise to me, and a painful one especially because I grew up at the foot of Kozara. Kozara epitomized brotherhood and humanity, the right feet of partisans, the valor of partisans, the tragedy, and in peace to have people from almost all over Yugoslavia came to Kozara to pay tribute to the monument and pay their respects and their homage. It also seemed very stage that Dr. Mladen Stojanovic, a partisan, a physician, a red doctor, and his monument is in front of the town hall in Prijedor and the song we always sang, he was killed by the traitors, Rade Radic and Chetniks, how could those Chetniks be something else now? It simply was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now the elections of 1990 were conducted across the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In Prijedor which parties competed for electoral positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor the competition was between the SDA and that was practically, if I may call it so, it did not have the word "Muslim" in its name because it was called the Party for Democratic Action, but it did bring together Muslims. Then SDS, Serb Democratic Party, which brought together Serbs. Then HDZ, the Croat Democratic Union, which rallied Croats, SDP which I think stands for Socialist Democratic Party, Reformists and the Party of Private Initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were the leaders of those parties? First of all, who were among the leaders of the SDA party in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Mirza Mujadzic was the leader of SDA. The SDS was for a very short while headed by a retired policeman called Milakovic, then Srdjo Srdic and then he was succeeded by Simo Miskovic. HDZ had Silvije Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the outcome of the 1990 election within the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can say is on the basis of the number of seats in our municipal town hall, I would not know that, but I know the seats in the municipal parliament. Of 90 seats 30 were won by SDA; 28 by SDS; two by HDZ, two by the party of Private Initiative and the rest I think were Reformists, SDP. So that altogether the chief two parties, SDA and SDS, were practically the winners because the difference of two seats would not mean any, if I may call it so, parliamentary victory because of those 90 seats one third were held by a reformist, that is the leftist side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were the political positions within the opstina then to be distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I covered the negotiations between SDA and SDS. I should say that they completely disregarded all the others who had won seats in the municipal parliament, and very quickly they agreed about the distribution of chief posts, that is the mayor, the deputy mayor, the head of the local government, the deputy, but then they got stuck when it came to some other posts. They agreed that the mayor of the municipality should come from the Party for Democratic Action and that was Muharem Cehajic. The deputy was to be appointed by SDS and that was Milomir Stakic. Then in the municipal government, in the opstina government, they had agreed that the President should be from SDS and that was Milorad Kovacevic and his deputy from SDA, that was Kulsumovic, I have just remembered, Kulsumovic, and then they said: "Well, it is most important that we agree about these chief posts, and then as we work we shall continue agreeing and we shall solve those problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As time went on was the Municipal Assembly able to resolve the problems concerning distribution of the remaining positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, they could not. They could not agree about two important positions in their view. That was the Director of the Public Auditing Service. This was something like financial control of the payments going through the Public Auditing Service. That was, no company, no firm, could run any business properly without, of course, taking care of one's public obligations. Then the problem with the Commander of the Police cropped up. I do not mean the public security station chief but I mean the security. Those sessions held were really painful, both to us who covered them and for those who listened to them and I should say the population of Prijedor at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now as those difficulties and the local assembly were occurring, first of all, were you familiar with what was happening at the republic level in the Republic Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was familiar with it. Television cameras, broadcast, press printed press, yes, they all covered it. As of the Serb communism, at the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia when the Croatian and Slavonia delegates left the Congress everything went downhill. Whether following someone's orders, whether it was good or not, but people I should say, all the people, all the Yugoslavs, all those in Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina included, wanted to know how the parliament operated, whether it be at the Federal Republican or municipal level. So that we had the opportunity to follow practically, to all intents and purposes, the intercourse of a parliamentary session at the Republican level, that is practically all their sessions. I should say there was no difference between the disagreements, discrepancies at the Republican level, that is in the Republican Assembly, or in the Municipal Assemblies. Misunderstandings or decisions in the Republican Parliament always found a reflection in the Municipal Assemblies, in Municipal Parliaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about the impact of the Croatian war as it was felt within opstina Prijedor. First of all, was there a call for mobilization in response to the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who responded to the mobilizations, members of which groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Muslims and Croats respond to the mobilizations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did, but I should say the number was insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What reasons or why did Muslims and Croats not respond to the mobilization when it occurred following the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not difficult to, it is not difficult to explain. Those who watched television or read newspapers, they could see more or less, not more or less, but precisely that it was not that Yugoslavia that was offered us, was not that Yugoslavia, it was something completely else that was merely disguised as Yugoslavia. I often read sentences that Yugoslavia was to be defended in Pakrac, in Lipik, in Croatia, in Slavonia, and many people, Muslims and Croats, pointed out that if one was to defend the borders, the frontiers of Yugoslavia, we shall all go, but why should we go to wage war in Croatia against the Croats since we live with them, since that is part of our state? I believe that the politicians of SDA or HDZ also had a part to play in that non-response to mobilization, but I believe that no matter how authoritative politicians were who tried to persuade the people not to respond to mobilization, that would not have born fruit simply because of what was happening in Croatia because those were not the boundaries of Yugoslavia; Yugoslavia was not an outside threat and it was difficult to go and fight against one people with another, that is decide with one people to fight against another people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of war had the JNA traditionally trained for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost throughout, I should say everywhere, in all places, in the media, at public meetings, in various places, it was always said that we are preparing for a defence war. I cannot but mention Tito who used to say, and I might say that this is the vestige of that, he used to say that one has to live in a manner as if there is never going to be another war, but that we always have to be ready as if a war might break out tomorrow. In no doctrines, that is there are no doctrines or text or at least I do not know of that, that the JNA was preparing for a war of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was this war seen by Muslims and Croats as a defensive war or a war of aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats saw it as an aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were Muslims and Croats able to see on television the manner in which the war was being conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were they able to hear from neighbours who came back from the war the manner in which it was being conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that play a role in the feelings against the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did Muslims and Croats understand what was happening in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats realised that this was greater Serbia in the making rather they maintained success stain news of the former Yugoslavia, because we could see tanks in Osjek or in Slovenia, how they were moving over passenger cars, and then soldiers of various ethnic origin were interviewed who happened to be there, who simply happened to be doing their regular military service and who said: "I do not know why I am in war. I do not know why I need this." In Vukovar there were young men from Prijedor who happened to be doing their military service and who took part in those attacks on Vukovar; some of them were killed. So it all played a role, and a good role at that. One simply did not want to go to war because he did not see, because one realised the substance and he saw that this was not the reason presented in public that that was the defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions about the way the war was covered by the local media. Was the coverage of the war by local media, Radio Prijedor, Kozarski Vjesnik, objective or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not objective. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the plebiscite as another reflection of the way in which the news was covered. What was the nature of that plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plebiscite was organised by the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS. They wanted to receive the agreement by the Serbian people asking them whether they wanted to remain in Yugoslavia or not. I think the plebiscite was organised in November 1991, but several things remind me of that plebiscite and they are related to this plebiscite. I did not go to the plebiscite, but I was told that those people who went to vote had two cards of two different colours: one for Serbs and the other for those who did not belong to the Serb people. The report in Kozarski Vjesnik was very good, very exhaustive, on two pages. On the first page there was a photograph and a big title: "The People Voted For". During the referendum which, if I remember, was held on 1st and 2nd March 1992 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the plebiscite was conducted by the SDS, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You described it as receiving extensive coverage in the local media and the public media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The referendum you referred to was the referendum for independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina which preceded its recognition by the international community; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. One of the conditions that had to be met by Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to be recognised was to organise a referendum so that all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina would state whether they were for an independent new state in that territory, a state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was an overwhelming vote in the favour of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor 57 or 58 per cent of the electorate took part in this referendum, and there was the qualified majority of more than 50 per cent for Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of coverage did that receive locally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In which media or do you mean generally in the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or at the radio and in the Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the local media.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the local media, as I said, as far as it goes for Kozarski Vjesnik there was a report from the referendum that was published in the sixth or seventh page. There were 12, maybe 15, lines not more than that, somewhere in the middle page which is a very, very big difference compared to the plebiscite where there were two full pages, the first and the second page, plus a photograph, plus a huge title say, "The People Voted for it. The people said Yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Up to 1992 were residents of Prijedor able to receive television broadcasts from Sarajevo as well as Belgrade and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very sensitive issue this about the media and informing. First of all, great problems were created: Why the region of Bosnian and Krajina could not easily follow and see the broadcast by Belgrade TV. I do not know exactly around what date, there was a problem, there was a transmitter taken by force and the transmitter called Lisina. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) he answered that the army promised that they would find the cause and that they would call him back. When the transmitter was taken on Kozara, the one called Lisina, those who took the transmitter, they could at any moment direct it in such a way as to choose which TV programme they could watch. In many cases we could see a football match broadcasted by TV Sarajevo, and then suddenly it would be interrupted and continued with the Belgrade news on Belgrade TV. So, in the region of the town and the municipality of Prijedor, you could see on the second channel the news broadcast by the Belgrade TV. Before that the Sarajevo TV would on the second channel broadcast the TV, the news from TV Zagreb and TV Belgrade, one after the other. After the transmitter was taken somebody, as I understood it, I understood like that, somebody wanted people to watch only the Belgrade TV news on the second channel. I went to Lisina. I am hiker and I used to go there. I could not understand, as we heard in the media, that a small group of some criminals that could do that when around that transmitter there was a fence and around it trees were cut so that the terrain was clear, there was a clearing. Nobody could have access to it without being seen from the inside. This is my conclusion. Theory the transmitter the JNA units were stationed. Later on we heard that that had been done by a group of people from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
